summary: Defines a parameter on the Content-Disposition header that marks which parts of a multipart MIME message the sender considers critical. A gateway to a less capable system can use that knowledge to handle multipart messages sensibly when it cannot deliver everything.

eli5.summary: If an email has many pieces and a poor delivery system can only pass some, this lets the sender mark the must-have pieces so they are not dropped.

questions: what is the mime handling parameter
what is the default value of handling in content-disposition
subtitle: A Content-Disposition parameter that lets a sender mark which message parts must arrive and which may be dropped.

tldr.problem: Gateways that connect Internet mail to less capable systems, such as voice mail, cannot always deliver every part of a multipart message. Without guidance they either reject the whole message or silently drop parts the sender cared about.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a Handling parameter to the Content-Disposition of a body part, set to REQUIRED or OPTIONAL. A content gateway fails the whole message if a REQUIRED part cannot pass, and may silently drop an OPTIONAL one.
tldr.outcome: The sender, not the gateway, decides what is expendable. Unmarked parts default to REQUIRED, so older senders keep the all-or-nothing behavior. The RFC updates RFC 3204 and is itself updated by RFC 5621.

today: RFC 3459 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3204 and has been updated by RFC 5621. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and the Content Gateway
sections.content:
RFC 3459 defines a way to mark body parts that a sender considers critical in a multipart Internet mail message. The mechanism is a parameter on the Content-Disposition header, as used by RFC 3204.

The need comes from linking Internet mail to systems that cannot render or store everything. The RFC's running example is a legacy voice messaging system: it may handle audio but not word processing files or video. A content gateway knows what the receiving system can handle. It passes what can be passed, may delete body parts that cannot be rendered or stored, and may reject a message the receiver cannot handle at all.

The RFC also notes that sender software may add body parts the sender never sees. Rejecting a message because of such a hidden part would confuse and upset the sender.
sections.eli5: A gateway is like a mail room at a building that cannot accept every kind of package. It needs to know which packages really matter to the sender.

sections.title: The Handling Parameter
sections.content:
The Handling parameter is inserted by the sending agent on a body part. It has two defined values.

  • Handling=REQUIRED means the part is critical. If the gateway cannot pass it, the entire message has failed and the gateway MUST take the appropriate failure action.
  • Handling=OPTIONAL means the sender does not care about notification reports for this part. If it cannot be passed, it may be silently deleted, and no delivery failure may be returned unless parts marked REQUIRED have also failed.

The default for a part with no marking is REQUIRED. That keeps existing notification behavior for senders that know nothing about the parameter. A gateway MUST treat unrecognized values as REQUIRED. The RFC floats a possible future value, IMPORTANT, but says no implementations do it.

The RFC uses the word REQUIRED as a parameter value, not in the RFC 2119 sense, and says so explicitly.
sections.eli5: Each item gets a sticker: 'must arrive' or 'fine to skip'. An item with no sticker counts as 'must arrive', just to be safe.

sections.title: Syntax and Registration
sections.content:
The collected syntax uses ABNF. The parameter name is handling, and its value is a notification-type: REQUIRED, OPTIONAL, another token, or a generic parameter. Both the parameter name and its values are not case sensitive.

RFC 3204 had already registered the Handling parameter. RFC 3459 repeats the registration for reference and as the normative place for other documents to point to. The allowable values listed are REQUIRED and OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: The label has a fixed wording, and it does not matter whether you write it in capitals or small letters.

sections.title: Notification Rules
sections.content:
The most obvious use is deciding whether to send a delivery or non-delivery notice. If the value is OPTIONAL, the gateway MUST NOT generate a notification. If it is REQUIRED, the gateway MAY generate one, following the normal request mechanisms such as the NOTIFY parameter on the SMTP RCPT command or the Disposition-Notification-To header. If a REQUIRED part fails and the sender asked for notification, the gateway MUST generate one for the whole message.

The kind of notice depends on the gateway's role. A gateway acting as a mail transfer agent generates a delivery status notification (DSN), which is the preferred option. A gateway acting as a mail user agent generates a message disposition notification (MDN). In SIP, the gateway returns a response code instead, and for the RFC 3204 case that is 415 (Unsupported Media Type) when the part is REQUIRED. When a notice is due because the receiver cannot render or store a media type, the status code is 5.6.1, 'Media not supported'.

The Handling marking alone does not guarantee any notification. Notification still follows the normal rules.
sections.eli5: If a 'skip me' item cannot be delivered, nobody gets a complaint. If a 'must arrive' item fails, the sender is told.

sections.title: Signed and Encrypted Content
sections.content:
For multipart/signed content, the indicator can go on the whole object, the signed content, the control (signature) part, or any mix. A REQUIRED mark on the signed enclosure means the sender wants true end-to-end verification, so the gateway must pass it intact, or reject the message if the lesser system cannot verify signatures. If the signature is OPTIONAL and the enclosed content REQUIRED, the gateway MAY strip the signature, though the RFC STRONGLY RECOMMENDS verifying it and flagging tampering where possible.

For multipart/encrypted content, marking the control object REQUIRED means the sender requires end-to-end encryption, so the gateway MUST reject the message if the endpoint cannot decrypt. If the control object is OPTIONAL, a gateway that can decrypt MAY forward cleartext, because the sender gave explicit permission. Since the default is REQUIRED, a sender who does nothing gets end-to-end encryption.
sections.eli5: If a letter is sealed and signed, the sender can say whether the seal must stay unbroken all the way, or whether the mail room may open it on the way.

sections.title: Interactions with Other MIME Types
sections.content:
Handling applies only to the selected alternative of a multipart/alternative. If that alternative is marked OPTIONAL, the gateway MUST NOT generate any delivery notifications, which shows that Handling overrides the DSN and MDN request mechanisms.

Criticality only affects the outermost level of a message, or the outermost level of the selected alternative. For message/rfc822 the receiving system ignores indicators in embedded body parts, so a forwarded message does not trigger or suppress unwanted reports. In multipart/related, the RFC's example is a Macintosh data fork and resource fork: for a Word document the data fork is likely critical and the resource fork can be ignored.
sections.eli5: Only the label on the outside box counts. Labels on boxes tucked inside a forwarded parcel are ignored.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Gateway between the Internet and a text-only short message service: a message has a text part marked REQUIRED and a tnef part. Knowing the service's limits, the gateway silently deletes the unmarked tnef part and passes the text. If no part had been marked, the whole message would be critical, so the tnef part would cause the gateway to reject it with a DSN carrying status code 5.6.1.

Three-part voice example: a text annotation, a voice message and a vCard, with the first two marked REQUIRED. If the receiving telephone interface cannot render text, the message fails even though the vCard failure alone would have been ignored. What happens next is implementation dependent. The RFC suggests holding the message for the user, or returning an MDN with disposition 'failed' and failure modifier 5.6.1.
sections.eli5: If the building only takes letters and your parcel has a letter plus a gift, the gift is quietly dropped, but only if you said the gift was optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending agents can use signatures over critical content indicators to protect the integrity of the indicator. The gateway MUST honor signature processing. If the sender marks signature components REQUIRED and the endpoint cannot do MIME signature processing, the gateway MUST establish an appropriate signature mechanism between itself and the endpoint, and it then becomes a target for tampering.

Receiving systems and users should not place any authentication value on the Handling parameter. By design, a gateway will silently delete unimportant parts at the sender's request, which lets the sender choose the acceptable level of integrity of what is delivered.
sections.eli5: The label tells the mail room what to do, but it is not proof of who sent the parcel, so nobody should trust the sticker as ID.
